unit.title: The Court and the Game
unit.summary: Objective, court map, kitchen, paddle and ball, singles vs doubles.

lessons.title: So what is pickleball?
lessons.objective: Say in one breath what pickleball is and why it isn't small tennis.

payload.prompt: Which is true about pickleball?

options.text: It combines elements of tennis, badminton and ping-pong

explanation.correct: Pickleball borrows from three sports but has unique rules (underhand serve, kitchen zone, two-bounce rule).
explanation.incorrect: Pickleball is not small tennis; the rules are fundamentally different.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's not just small tennis, the rules are totally different.

payload.prompt: What was pickleball invented as?

explanation.correct: Pickleball started in 1965 on Bainbridge Island, Washington as a backyard game.
explanation.incorrect: It was a casual backyard invention, not a planned sport.
explanation.sayThisLine: It started as a backyard game, now it's everywhere.

payload.prompt: Why is the serve underhand in pickleball?

options.text: Overhand serves would hurt your shoulder
The rules require it, so the serve is not a power weapon
Paddles are too small for overhand serves

explanation.correct: The rules require an underhand swing, so a strong server cannot win the point outright. That keeps rallies going and favours placement over power.
explanation.incorrect: The underhand serve is a rule, not a matter of comfort or paddle size. It is there so the serve starts the rally rather than ending it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The serve is underhand, so the rally is the point, not the serve.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: The rules are actually really different
Not at all, totally different game
It's small tennis for old people

payload.translation: A very common guess. The kitchen, the underhand serve, the scoring and the court size are all different, so share that warmly rather than correcting.

followUps.line: The rules are actually really different, especially the kitchen and the serve.
It looks similar but the strategy is totally different.
followUps.why: Acknowledges the surface resemblance but sets expectations.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to explain everything at once; just correct the misconception gently.

lessons.title: The court, measured
lessons.objective: Locate the net, baselines, sidelines and centerline; know the size.

payload.prompt: How wide is a pickleball court in feet?

explanation.correct: Twenty feet wide and 44 long, the same size as a doubles badminton court.
explanation.incorrect: It is 20 feet wide and 44 feet long. It is a small court, which is why the game is so compact.

payload.prompt: How tall is the net at the center of the court in inches?

explanation.correct: The net is 36 inches at the posts and 34 inches at the center (slightly lower in the middle).
explanation.incorrect: The net is 34 inches at the center, 36 at the posts, lower than tennis.

payload.prompt: Tap the centerline.

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court. The net runs across the middle with service boxes on each side.

explanation.correct: The centerline splits the left and right service boxes behind the kitchen. It stops at the kitchen line; it does not run through the kitchen.
explanation.incorrect: Look behind the kitchen, down the middle between the two service boxes. That is the centerline.
explanation.sayThisLine: The centerline splits the service boxes behind the kitchen.

payload.prompt: What does the centerline do?

explanation.correct: The centerline runs from the kitchen line back to the baseline and splits the left and right service boxes. It is what makes a serve land in the correct diagonal box.
explanation.incorrect: The centerline is the line between the two service boxes behind the kitchen. It does not mark the net and it does not separate singles from doubles, because the court is the same size for both.
explanation.sayThisLine: The centerline splits the service boxes.

lessons.title: Kitchen and service boxes
lessons.objective: Map the kitchen and the four service boxes.

payload.prompt: Tap the kitchen zones.

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court. The net runs across the middle with shaded kitchen zones on either side.

explanation.correct: The kitchen is the seven-foot strip on each side of the net. No volleys in it.
explanation.incorrect: Look next to the net. That short strip on each side is the kitchen.
explanation.sayThisLine: The kitchen is right beside the net on each side.

payload.prompt: Match the court zones.

pairs.definition: The 7-foot zone where you cannot volley
The back boundary of the court
The line at the far edge of the kitchen, 7 feet from the net

distractorDefinitions: The line where doubles players stand

explanation.summary: Kitchen is the NVZ, service boxes are where serves land, baseline is the back, kitchen line marks the kitchen edge.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kitchen, service box, baseline and kitchen line all have specific purposes.

payload.prompt: Can you volley on the kitchen line?

scene.alt: You stand with a toe on the kitchen line and the ball is coming over the net without having bounced.

explanation.correct: The kitchen line counts as kitchen; a toe on it means you cannot volley.
explanation.incorrect: The line is part of the kitchen for volley rules, so wait for the bounce.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kitchen line is kitchen, so no volley.

payload.prompt: What is the kitchen rule mainly there to stop?

options.text: Players smashing volleys from right at the net
Players ever stepping into that zone
The ball bouncing near the net
Serves landing in the service boxes

explanation.correct: Without it, a tall player could stand at the net and smash everything. Banning volleys in the zone forces soft shots near the net, which rewards patience over power.
explanation.incorrect: You can stand in the kitchen and the ball can bounce there. The rule only bans volleys from inside it, and that is what creates the soft game.
explanation.sayThisLine: The kitchen keeps it patient, not a smashing fest.

lessons.title: Lines are in
lessons.objective: Know that baseline, sideline, centerline count as in.

payload.prompt: The ball lands right on the baseline.

scene.alt: Ball touching the far baseline of the pickleball court.

explanation.correct: Lines are in. Any part of the ball touching a boundary line counts as in.
explanation.incorrect: A ball touching the baseline is in. Only the kitchen line has a special rule for serves.
explanation.sayThisLine: If it touches the line, it's in.

payload.prompt: The ball lands on the sideline.

explanation.correct: Sidelines are in. The ball is in play if any part touches the line.
explanation.incorrect: The sideline is in bounds. Any touch of the line means the ball is in.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sidelines are in, just like baselines.

payload.prompt: Which lines count as 'in'?

options.text: All lines except the kitchen line (on serves)

explanation.correct: Baseline, sideline and centerline are in. For serves, the kitchen line is out (short serve). For volleys, the kitchen line is kitchen (fault).
explanation.incorrect: All lines are in except the kitchen line on a serve, which is short (a fault).
explanation.sayThisLine: Lines are in, except the kitchen line on a serve.

payload.prompt: Complete the rule about lines.
payload.template: When the ball touches a {{location}}, it counts as {{status}}.

explanation.correct: Any touch of a boundary line (baseline, sideline, centerline) means the ball is in.
explanation.incorrect: Lines are in bounds. Any contact with the line means the ball is in play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Touch the line and it's in.

lessons.title: Paddle and ball
lessons.objective: Recognize a legal paddle and ball and why the ball has holes.

payload.prompt: Which ball is built for outdoor play?

image.alt: Two plastic balls side by side. The left ball has a few large round holes. The right ball has many small holes.

explanation.correct: Outdoor balls have more, smaller holes and are harder, so wind bothers them less.
explanation.incorrect: Look at the holes. Many small holes mean outdoor; a few large holes mean indoor.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about the holes.
payload.template: The holes add air drag, so the ball moves {{speed}} than a solid ball and gives you {{time}} to react.

explanation.correct: The holes add air drag, so the ball flies slower and gives players time to react and rally. A solid ball would be much harder to control on such a small court.
explanation.incorrect: The holes add air drag, which slows the ball. That is what makes long rallies on a small court possible.
explanation.sayThisLine: Holes in the ball slow it down, that's the whole design.

payload.prompt: What is a legal paddle size limit?

options.text: 17 inches length max, 24 inches combined length and width max

explanation.correct: A paddle is legal if it is 17 inches long max and 24 inches combined length and width.
explanation.incorrect: Paddles are smaller than tennis racquets. The legal limit is 24 inches combined dimensions.
explanation.sayThisLine: Paddles have size limits so nobody gets crazy with the equipment.

payload.prompt: Which is a pickleball paddle?

image.alt: Three racquets: a small hard paddle, a tennis racquet and a badminton racquet.

explanation.correct: The pickleball paddle is small, hard and flat, nothing like a tennis racquet.
explanation.incorrect: A pickleball paddle is much smaller than a tennis racquet and has a hard, flat face.

lessons.title: Singles or doubles
lessons.objective: Explain why doubles dominates and what changes in singles.

payload.prompt: Which is the standard format in pickleball?

explanation.correct: Doubles is the standard format in recreational and pro pickleball; singles is rarer and more tiring.
explanation.incorrect: Pickleball is a doubles sport. Singles is rare and exhausting because one person covers the whole court.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pickleball is a doubles game, singles is brutal.

payload.prompt: In singles, is there a "server two"?

scene.alt: Two players on opposite sides of the court in a singles game.

choices.label: No, serve until you lose a rally

explanation.correct: Singles has no partner, so there is no second server. You serve until you lose a rally, then the serve goes to your opponent.
explanation.incorrect: Server one and server two only exist in doubles, where a partner gets a turn. In singles the serve simply passes to the opponent when the server loses a rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: In singles you just serve until you lose a rally.

payload.prompt: Three players are here. Singles or doubles?

situation.narrative: Friendly open play. You feel fit and want a good game.

options.label: Wait for the fourth and play doubles
options.consequence: Four players are on court soon, everyone gets a game, and it stays social and less tiring.
considerations: Doubles is the standard recreational format
Shared court is less tiring and more forgiving

options.label: Play singles now and rotate in the third player
options.consequence: You get a game right away, but one friend waits and singles covers far more court.
considerations: Fine when only two can play
Someone sits out while you wait

options.label: Insist on competitive singles against one friend
options.consequence: The third friend is left out and the game turns into a tiring workout, not a friendly game.
considerations: Singles suits two players who both choose it

payload.expertNote: Doubles is the heart of pickleball: social, less tiring, and forgiving. Choose singles when only two players are there, or both want the extra court coverage.
payload.sayThisLine: Let's wait for a fourth and play doubles.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about why doubles is so popular.
payload.template: In doubles you {{share}} the court with a partner, so it is more {{mood}} and less tiring than singles.

explanation.correct: Two players split the court, so you get a partner to talk to and less ground to cover. That is why most games you will see or hear about are doubles.
explanation.incorrect: It comes down to sharing: a partner splits the running and makes it a social game. Singles is a fine game, just harder work per person.
explanation.sayThisLine: Doubles is more fun because you have a partner.

lessons.title: How a point plays out
lessons.objective: Order a rally: serve, return, third shot, then free play.

payload.prompt: Put a rally's opening in order.

items.text: Serve lands in the diagonal box
items.why: Every rally begins with an underhand serve.

items.text: Receiver returns after the serve bounces
items.why: The return must bounce first (two-bounce rule).

items.text: Serving team hits the third shot after the return bounces
items.why: The two-bounce rule applies to both sides.

items.text: Now anyone may volley (not in the kitchen)
items.why: After two bounces, volleys are legal outside the kitchen.

explanation.correct: Serve, return, third shot, then free play. That is why the third shot is such a big deal.
explanation.incorrect: The opening always runs serve, return, third shot. Only then may anyone volley.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's all about the third shot.

payload.prompt: What is the two-bounce rule?

options.text: The ball must bounce twice total
The serve and return must each bounce before anyone may volley
You must bounce the ball before hitting it

explanation.correct: Two-bounce rule: the serve bounces on the receiving side, the return bounces on the serving side, then volleys are allowed.
explanation.incorrect: It is two bounces, one on each side. That is the two-bounce rule, and it stops the serving team from rushing the net.
explanation.sayThisLine: The serve bounces, the return bounces, then the volleying starts.

payload.prompt: You served. Their return is coming back in the air.

scene.alt: You stand near the baseline. The return of serve is coming at you in the air.

explanation.correct: Two-bounce rule: the return has to bounce on your side before your team may hit it.
explanation.incorrect: The serving team must let the return bounce first. Only then can volleys start.
explanation.sayThisLine: The return has to bounce on our side before we can hit it.

payload.title: How a point plays out

exchanges.theirMessage: The serve bounced, the return bounced, then we started volleying.

replies.text: So two bounces before anyone could volley?
replies.coachNote: You named the two-bounce rule correctly.

replies.text: Cool, so then you won the point?
replies.coachNote: Fine, but you could have asked about the two-bounce part.

replies.text: Why didn't you just volley the serve back?
replies.theirResponse: Because it's the rule, and it's the whole strategy.
replies.coachNote: The two-bounce rule is fundamental; respect it.

payload.closingNote: Every rally starts serve, return, third shot, then volleys. The third shot is the key moment.
